client: I lost my grandmother about a month ago, and honestly, I didn't expect it to hit me this hard. Some days I can barely get through basic things like making breakfast or answering emails because my mind just keeps drifting back to her. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist:
It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that what you're feeling makes complete sense. Losing your grandmother is a profound loss, and the way grief quietly pulls you away from everyday tasks isn't a sign that something is wrong with you; it's a sign of how deeply she mattered. 

I'm really glad you decided to try something, and I'm here to go at whatever pace feels right for you — so I'm wondering, when your mind drifts back to her during those quiet moments, what kinds of memories or thoughts tend to come up most?

client: Mostly I keep thinking about the last time I saw her, and how I was kind of distracted and in a rush to leave. I keep replaying that visit and wishing I had stayed longer, just sat with her more instead of checking my phone or thinking about work stuff. It's like my brain won't let me remember the good times without circling back to that one afternoon and making me feel like I failed her somehow.
therapist:
That feeling of "I failed her" is such a painful place for your mind to keep landing, and I want to gently reflect something back to you — the fact that you're hurting this much over one distracted afternoon is itself evidence of how much you loved her and how present you *wanted* to be in her life. Our minds often latch onto the one moment that feels imperfect while glossing over the countless moments where you showed up for her in ways that mattered.

I'm curious — if a close friend came to you carrying this exact same guilt about *their* grandmother, what would you say to them about that one afternoon?

client: I know what you're getting at, and honestly if a friend told me this I'd probably say something like "one bad afternoon doesn't erase everything else, you were there for her in so many ways." But it feels different when it's me, like I can give that grace to someone else easily but I just can't seem to apply it to myself. I don't know if that's just how guilt works or if there's actually something more to it in my case, because part of me still feels like my situation was somehow worse than a hypothetical friend's.
therapist:
You've just noticed something really important — that you can access wisdom and compassion easily for others, but there's a part of you that feels your situation deserves a harsher verdict, like you're a special exception to the grace you'd offer anyone else. That's actually a very common pattern in grief and guilt, where our mind works overtime to build a case against us, cherry-picking evidence that "proves" we fell short while dismissing the rest. 

I'd love to gently explore that feeling that your situation was somehow worse — what is it about that afternoon specifically that makes it feel like it crosses a line that a hypothetical friend's wouldn't?

client: I think part of what makes it feel worse is that I had this nagging feeling even that day that I should slow down and be more present, like some part of me knew time with her was precious, and I ignored it anyway. So it's not just that I was distracted, it's that I made a conscious choice in that moment to prioritize other things, and that feels harder to forgive than just accidentally zoning out. I guess I'm worried that if I let myself off the hook, it means I'm just making excuses for something that was genuinely selfish.
therapist:
What you're describing actually shows a kind of moral seriousness and self-awareness that speaks well of you — you *had* that instinct to be present, which means you genuinely valued that time with her, even if in that moment you couldn't fully act on it. There's an important difference between forgiving yourself and making excuses: forgiving yourself means acknowledging the full truth — yes, you made a choice you wish you hadn't, *and* you were a loving grandchild who showed up for her in countless other ways — rather than letting one afternoon become the whole story. 

I'm wondering, do you think your grandmother, knowing everything she knew about you and your relationship, would agree that that one afternoon defined who you were to her?

client: No, she wouldn't have seen it that way, I know that logically. She was always the kind of person who focused on the love underneath things rather than the small moments where someone fell short, and honestly she probably didn't even register that afternoon the way I have. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling it are two completely different things, and I'm not sure how to get those two to line up, because right now my feelings are just louder than my logic.
therapist:
You've just named one of the most honest and important truths about how we work — that knowing something and *feeling* it are genuinely different experiences, and it's not a failure of willpower or intelligence that they don't automatically match up. The good news is that this gap isn't permanent; feelings tend to shift gradually as we gently and repeatedly offer them new experiences and evidence, rather than just trying to think our way out of them in one go.

I'm curious — are there any specific memories of your grandmother, moments where you *did* slow down and really show up for her, that your mind hasn't been visiting as often as that last afternoon?

client: There are some memories, yeah, like there was this whole stretch a few years back where I would drive to her place every Sunday and we'd cook together and she'd tell me stories about her childhood that I never got tired of hearing. I haven't been letting myself think about those much, maybe because they make me sad in a different way, like I'm grieving what we had rather than just feeling guilty. I guess I've been so focused on that last afternoon that I've almost been avoiding the good memories, which is strange when I think about it out loud.
therapist:
What you just noticed — that you've been avoiding the good memories — is a really meaningful insight, and it makes a kind of painful sense: those Sunday cooking sessions represent the fullness of what you had with her, and letting yourself feel that love and loss all at once is a lot to hold. But those memories of driving to her place, cooking together, listening to her stories for hours — that *is* who you were to her, far more than any distracted afternoon could ever undo.

I wonder if, sometime this week, you might gently allow yourself to sit with one of those Sunday memories — not to push the grief away, but just to let that version of your relationship take up a little more space alongside the guilt — and notice what comes up for you?

client: I want to try that, but I'm a little worried that sitting with those memories intentionally will just make me cry and feel worse, and then I'll have to go on with my day feeling raw and undone. It's almost easier to stay in the guilt because at least that feels like I'm doing something, like I'm holding myself accountable, whereas just remembering the good times feels like it might just open up how much I miss her without any real purpose. I guess I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with all of that feeling once it comes up.
therapist:
What you just said about guilt feeling productive — like you're "doing something" — is such a perceptive observation, and it helps explain why your mind has been holding onto it so tightly, because grief without a task can feel frighteningly shapeless. But here's a gentle reframe: letting yourself cry and miss her *is* doing something — it's actually the work of grief, and those tears aren't a sign that you're falling apart, they're a sign that the love you had for her is still real and alive in you. 

Maybe the goal of sitting with a good memory doesn't need to be to feel better afterward, but simply to let yourself fully acknowledge what you had with her — and I'm wondering, is there a small, contained moment in your day, even just five minutes, where feeling a little raw might actually be okay and safe enough to try?

client: Maybe early in the morning before the day really starts, like when I'm having my first cup of coffee, that might be the one time where I'm not already bracing for something or in the middle of a task. I think I could try five minutes then, though I'm honestly not sure I can control when the crying stops once it starts, and I have to go to work after. I guess I'm worried about opening a door I can't close in time.
therapist:
That early morning coffee window sounds like a genuinely wise choice — you already know it as a quieter, softer part of your day, and there's something fitting about honoring her memory in a moment of stillness. About the fear of not being able to close the door in time — many people find that grief, when we actually turn toward it intentionally rather than being ambushed by it, tends to feel more manageable than when it catches us off guard, and having a small ritual to gently close the moment, like finishing your coffee or stepping outside for a breath of fresh air, can help signal to yourself that it's okay to return to the day. 

Would you be open to trying it just once this week, and maybe noticing whether the feeling of being "undone" afterward is as uncontrollable as you're anticipating, or whether it surprises you in some way?

client: Yeah, I think I can try it once, just once, and see what happens. The idea of having a small ritual to close it actually helps a little, like finishing my coffee as a kind of signal, because otherwise it just feels like I'd be floating in it with no way out. I'm still nervous, but I guess one morning isn't going to break me, and maybe I'll learn something about whether I can actually handle this better than I think I can.
therapist:
That shift you just made — from "I can't handle this" to "maybe I can handle this better than I think" — is a small but really meaningful one, and I want you to notice that you arrived there yourself just by talking it through. One morning, one cup of coffee, one memory — that's exactly the right size for this experiment, and whatever happens, you'll have learned something true about yourself rather than just imagining the worst. 

When you come back, I'd love to hear how it went — not whether you cried or didn't, or whether it felt "successful," but just what it was like to give yourself that five minutes with her.

client: That actually means something to me, that you're not grading it on whether I cried or held it together, because I think that's been part of what's made grief feel so exhausting, like I'm supposed to be doing it correctly somehow. I'm still a little skeptical that five minutes is going to shift anything major, but I think I needed someone to give me permission to just feel it without it having to lead somewhere productive. I'll try it, and I guess I'll see what she has to say to me when I let myself actually think about her for a minute.
therapist:
There's no right way to grieve, and the fact that you've been carrying this invisible pressure to do it correctly on top of the loss itself — that's an exhausting weight you didn't need to be holding. And that last thing you said, about seeing what she has to say to you — I find that really beautiful, because it sounds like some part of you already knows her voice is still there, waiting in those memories you've been keeping at a distance.

I'll be here when you're ready to share what that morning was like for you — and I hope you can carry a little of that same grace into the week that you so easily offered your imaginary friend earlier today.
